extracted.subtask_description: A beginner-focused guide describing common German greetings and goodbyes, when and where to use them, and appropriate responses and formality levels. Covers regional variations, time-of-day forms, and phone/text conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hallo — “Hello”
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest, friendly all-purpose greeting usable in pretty much any situation, formal or informal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'hallo' as a general-purpose greeting. It is appropriate in most contexts and works for both formal and informal encounters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guten Tag — “Good day” (time-of-day greetings & grammar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slightly formal 'hello' commonly known to English speakers; part of a set of time-of-day greetings (guten Morgen, guten Tag, guten Abend).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose by time of day: before midday use 'guten Morgen'; midday until ~6pm 'guten Tag'; 6pm until bedtime 'guten Abend'. Note grammar: 'guten' is the masculine accusative form of 'gut' because the phrase implies 'I wish you a good day' (ich wünsche dir einen guten Tag), so the adjective takes accusative. This explains why it's 'guten Tag' not 'gut Tag'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alles klar — “All clear” (informal greeting)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Alles klar' literally means 'everything (is) clear!' and is used frequently, especially by young people, as a greeting similar to 'what's up?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be used as a question ('alles klar?'), a statement, or filler. Best reply is a simple 'ja' or 'ja, alles klar, danke' ('yes, everything is good, thanks'). Treat it like an informal conversational opener rather than a literal question requiring details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Was ist los? — “What’s up?” (ambiguous: greeting or concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Was ist los?' can mean 'what's up?' or 'what's the matter?' depending on context and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone and situation determine meaning. As a greeting it functions like 'what's up?' and typically doesn't require a long answer. Be aware it can also express concern; use context to interpret whether a genuine problem is being asked about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wie geht es dir? — “How’s it going?” (formality/pronoun choices & responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common way to ask 'how's it going?' Informal singular uses 'dir'; formal uses 'wie geht es Ihnen?'; informal plural uses 'wie geht es euch?'. Often shortened to 'wie geht's?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'dir' for informal one-on-one, 'Ihnen' in formal situations, and 'euch' addressing an informal group. Typical short reply is 'gut, danke' ('good, thanks'). Remember appropriate pronoun choice to match formality and number of people addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grüß Gott! — regional formal greeting (Bavaria/Austria)
rubrics_metrics.description: A greeting mainly used in Bavaria and Austria; literally something like 'greetings (from) God' and often rendered 'God bless you'. Very formal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in south-eastern Germany and Austria. There's a less formal local variant 'Grüß dich!' (greetings to you) used more by older people. Be mindful of regional and generational differences in acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Servus — regional greeting/goodbye (Bavaria/Austria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally Latin for 'servant'; used as a greeting in Bavaria and Austria and can also be used to say goodbye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate in southern German-speaking areas. Note it functions both as hello and goodbye depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moin! — northern Germany greeting (any time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common greeting in northern Germany (around Hamburg), sometimes doubled as 'moin moin!'. Can be used at any time of day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safe to use at all hours in northern regions like Schleswig-Holstein and Hamburg. Origins uncertain (possibly from 'Morgen' or Low German word for 'good'). Using it signals regional friendliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Na — short northern greeting/exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Na' is a brief northern German greeting that can mean 'hi', 'how are you?', and 'fine thanks, how are you?' all in one; it's hard to translate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by northern Germans as a versatile opener. Typical exchange: one says 'na', the other replies 'na', and conversation follows. It functions as a casual, efficient greeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hier ist… — identifying yourself when not face-to-face
rubrics_metrics.description: When calling, texting, or otherwise contacting someone at a distance, use 'hier ist [Name]' to say 'it's [Name]' (you can't directly translate 'it's Benny' as 'es ist Benny').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'hier ist [Name]' to identify yourself on the phone or in messages to someone who already knows you but may not recognise your voice/number. This is a subtle but important colloquial convention in German.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tschüss — informal goodbye
rubrics_metrics.description: A common casual way to say 'bye' in German.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronunciation note: 'tsch' sounds like English 'ch'. Use 'Tschüss' in informal settings as the usual parting phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ciao — borrowed informal goodbye
rubrics_metrics.description: Italian in origin but commonly used in Germany as an informal goodbye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works like other casual farewells; reflects cross-European usage. Use informally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auf Wiedersehen — formal 'see you again' (old-fashioned)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Auf Wiedersehen' literally 'when we see each other again'; understood by all but sounds formal and somewhat old-fashioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate for formal contexts or when you want to be polite/formal; may come across as stiff in casual company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bis bald — informal 'see you soon'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Bis bald' literally means 'until soon' and is a friendly informal way to say 'see you soon'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use with acquaintances and friends when you expect to see them again in the near future; conveys friendliness and informality.
